product.name: ModelSpec
product.eyebrow: The goal: training compiled for one target · M1
promise: Compile it into a runtime built for one GPU, to train faster.
product.lede: ModelSpec is for training models faster than a general-purpose framework can; that speed is the goal and not shipped yet. Model, loss, gradients, optimizer and data are one typed .mspec program, so the compiler knows the whole step before it runs and can build a runtime for one use case, one operating system and one GPU, and every optimization is checked against a CPU reference. Today it trains on one Vulkan GPU, an RTX 3090, where a transformer step is still many times slower than PyTorch's. No Python, PyTorch or CUDA.
product.meta: One Rust binary · CPU reference and Vulkan training · Apache-2.0

art.caption: The repository's example checked and trained on the CPU reference. Recorded by modelspec-docs from the modelspec command line, not typed.

sections.title: Faster training, because nothing is general at run time.
sections.lede: A general-purpose framework has to stay general while it runs. A ModelSpec runtime is compiled for one program on one target, and a compiler change that alters a result is refused. Faster than PyTorch is the planned outcome; the BERT-tiny ladder measures it.

items.title: The compiler knows the whole step
items.description: Model, loss, gradients, optimizer, data bindings and execution policy are one declared, typed program. Forward pass, loss, backward pass and update compile into one verified Training IR program before anything runs.

items.title: A runtime for one target
items.description: Compile that program into a runtime specialised for one use case, one operating system and one GPU chipset. One target exists today: Vulkan compute and SPIR-V on one RTX 3090 on Linux, with the kernel plan scheduled for its device profile. Runtimes for other systems and chipsets are planned.

items.title: Optimizations that cannot change a result
items.description: Every kernel, fusion and pass is checked against the CPU reference interpreter on the same IR. A faster change is kept; a change that alters a result is refused. That makes aggressive optimization safe to try, by people or agents.

items.title: BERT-tiny against PyTorch, step by step
items.description: Today ModelSpec is slower: the BERT-tiny encoder block at batch 8 takes 93,868.4 µs per step on the RTX 3090 against 3,937.2 µs on PyTorch eager. Planned: the block within 3× of PyTorch eager, then full BERT-tiny at parity, then faster than torch.compile.

sections.title: Errors before anything runs.
sections.lede: A declarative, statically typed language and a Rust compiler for differentiable tensor programs. A shape mismatch is a compile error with both operand types, not an exception halfway through training.

items.title: Shapes in the types
items.description: Every tensor is Tensor<f32, [dims]>, or Tensor<i32, [dims]> for row ids and labels. matmul, add, mse and the other operators check their operands' shapes, and a mismatch names both types and the dimension it expected.

items.title: Reproducible from the seed
items.description: Parameters and synthetic data are drawn from the train block's seed and each parameter's canonical path. Two runs with the same seed print identical bytes.

items.title: A stable code for every diagnostic
items.description: Each refusal starts with a code such as E-TYPE-012, declared next to the stage that emits it and listed with its meaning in the reference.

items.title: Gradients checked against finite differences
items.description: Every gradient rule of the operator registry is tested against central finite differences in f64 on the CPU reference.

items.title: GPU training through Vulkan and SPIR-V
items.description: modelspec train --backend vulkan runs SPIR-V kernels generated in Rust on one device through the system Vulkan loader, within the GPU tolerance of the CPU reference, since 0.4.0.

items.title: A small BERT, from scratch
items.description: Embedding, attention, layer norm, GELU, dropout and the masked-language-model loss run on the CPU reference and, since 0.17.0, as Vulkan kernels; the data commands pack a corpus into token sequences, and BERT-tiny pre-trained on one RTX 3090 ends below the unigram baseline.

sections.eyebrow: One file to a trained model
sections.title: Parse, check, lower, differentiate, train.
sections.lede: Each stage hands a verified value to the next. The CPU interpreter and the Vulkan backend run the same Training IR.
